plan: [ In a second-price sealed-bid auction with independent private values, bidding your true value is a weakly dominant strategy. It maximizes expected profit by ensuring you win exactly when the second-highest bid is below your value, and you pay that second-highest bid, not your own. With only 1 round and no history to exploit, there’s no benefit to strategic shading or bluffing. My value is $7, so I will bid exactly $7 to ensure I neither overpay nor miss positive-surplus wins. ]

[ This is a sealed-bid, second-price auction with independent private values uniformly distributed. In such auctions, bidding your true value is a weakly dominant strategy: it maximizes expected profit regardless of others’ strategies. Shading risks losing when winning would be profitable, and overbidding risks negative payoff if the second price exceeds value. With no informative history and only one round, no learning applies. Therefore, bid exactly my value ($32). If tied at the top, the random tie-break is acceptable because expected payoff remains nonnegative when bidding truthfully. ]

[Second-price auction with 3 bidders and independent private values. Truthful bidding is weakly dominant: overbidding can win when the second-highest bid exceeds my value (negative payoff), and underbidding can forfeit positive surplus when I would have won paying below my value. There’s no exploitable history (round 1 of 1). To maximize expected profit, bid exactly my value, $15, ensuring I only win when the second-highest bid is ≤15, yielding nonnegative surplus equal to 15 minus that bid.]
